hmmt-feb-2004-team-01.title: Induction
hmmt-feb-2004-team-01.body:
We use induction on $n$. Row $0$ consists of a single $1$ and zeros, and each entry of row $1$ is a sum of two distinct entries of row $0$, so it is at most $1=2^0$.

Suppose every number in row $n$ is at most $2^{n-1}$. Each number in row $n+1$ is a sum of two numbers of row $n$, so it is at most $2^{n-1}+2^{n-1}=2^n$. This completes the induction. ∎

hmmt-feb-2004-team-02.title: Lower bound and construction
hmmt-feb-2004-team-02.body:
By the previous bound, every number in row $n$ is at most $2^{n-1}$ (for $n>0$). Since $2^{10}=1024<2004\le2048=2^{11}$, a number as large as $2004$ cannot appear before row $12$.

Row $12$ is possible: start the table as follows, writing only the three relevant entries of each row, and in each row choose each entry as the sum of two of the three entries above it (and its neighbours):
$$\begin{array}{l}
\text{row }0:\ 1\\
\text{row }1:\ 1,1\\
\text{row }2:\ 1,2,2\\
\text{row }3:\ 3,4,4\\
\text{row }4:\ 7,8,8\\
\text{row }5:\ 15,16,16\\
\text{row }6:\ 31,31,32\\
\text{row }7:\ 62,63,63\\
\text{row }8:\ 125,125,126\\
\text{row }9:\ 250,251,251\\
\text{row }10:\ 501,501,502\\
\text{row }11:\ 1002,1002,1003\\
\text{row }12:\ 2004,2004,2005
\end{array}$$
(For instance, row $12$'s first entry is $1002+1002$, its second is $1002+1002$ and its third is $1002+1003$; the entries beyond these three are $0$ in every row.) Row $12$ contains $2004$.

**Answer: 12**

hmmt-feb-2004-team-03.title: Hint, then induction
hmmt-feb-2004-team-03.body:
*The hint.* For $n\ge2$ and $r\ge2$:
$$S(n-1,r-1)+S(n-1,r)=\sum_{i=r-1}^{n-1}\binom{n-2}{i-1}+\sum_{i=r-1}^{n-1}\binom{n-2}{i}=\sum_{i=r-1}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{i}=S(n,r),$$
by Pascal's rule (with $\binom{n-2}{n-1}=0$).

*Monotonicity.* From the definition, $S(m,s)=S(m,s+1)+\binom{m-1}{s-1}\ge S(m,s+1)$, so $S(m,\cdot)$ is non-increasing in $s$.

*Induction on $n$.* For $n=1$: the entry one column to the left of the original $1$ is at most $1=S(1,1)$, and entries $r\ge2$ columns to the left are $0=S(1,r)$, since row $1$ is nonzero only in columns adjacent to the top $1$.

Assume the claim for row $n-1$. Consider the entry in row $n$, $r$ columns to the left of the original $1$.
- If $r=1$, the claim reads "at most $S(n,1)=2^{n-1}$", which is the previous problem.
- If $r\ge2$, the entry is a sum of two of the three entries above it, which are $r-1$, $r$ and $r+1$ columns to the left in row $n-1$. By the induction hypothesis they are at most $S(n-1,r-1)$, $S(n-1,r)$ and $S(n-1,r+1)$, and by monotonicity these are in decreasing order. So the sum of two of them is at most $S(n-1,r-1)+S(n-1,r)=S(n,r)$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2004-team-04.title: Sum the bounds
hmmt-feb-2004-team-04.body:
Entries more than $n$ columns from the centre are $0$. By the bound $S(n,r)$, the total of the entries to the left of the central column is at most
$$\sum_{r=1}^{n}S(n,r)=\sum_{r=1}^n\sum_{i=r-1}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}i=\sum_{s=0}^{n-1}(s+1)\binom{n-1}{s},$$
since $\binom{n-1}s$ appears for the $s+1$ values $r=1,\dots,s+1$. Call this sum $T$. Reversing the order of summation ($s\to n-1-s$),
$$2T=\sum_{s=0}^{n-1}\bigl((s+1)+(n-s)\bigr)\binom{n-1}s=(n+1)2^{n-1},$$
so $T=(n+1)2^{n-2}$.

The mirror image of a valid table is a valid table, so the same bound holds for the entries to the right of the central column. The central entry is at most $2^{n-1}$. So the row sum is at most
$$2\cdot(n+1)2^{n-2}+2^{n-1}=(n+1)2^{n-1}+2^{n-1}=(n+2)2^{n-1}.\ ∎$$

hmmt-feb-2004-team-05.title: Charge pairs to odd numbers
hmmt-feb-2004-team-05.body: Every switch pair contains exactly one odd number. An odd number has only two neighbours, so it belongs to at most two switch pairs. Hence the number of switch pairs is at most twice the number of odd numbers. ∎

hmmt-feb-2004-team-06.title: Find a switch pair above each odd number
hmmt-feb-2004-team-06.body:
Each odd number in row $n$ is the sum of two of the three numbers above it (in row $n-1$, in three consecutive positions). These three numbers cannot all have the same parity: otherwise any sum of two of them would be even. So among them there are two adjacent entries of different parity, i.e. a switch pair within the three.

Now a switch pair in row $n-1$ occupying positions $j,j+1$ lies among the three entries above position $c$ only if $c\in\{j,j+1\}$, so it can be assigned to at most two numbers of row $n$. Therefore the number of odd numbers in row $n$ is at most twice the number of switch pairs in row $n-1$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2004-team-07.title: Runs of odd numbers
hmmt-feb-2004-team-07.body:
Far enough to the left and right every entry is $0$ (even). So the odd entries of row $n$ form finitely many *runs* (maximal blocks of consecutive odd numbers), each surrounded by even numbers. Each run contributes exactly two switch pairs (one at each end), and there are no other switch pairs. So the number of switch pairs in row $n$ equals $2R$, where $R$ is the number of runs.

Take a run and let $c$ be the position of its first (leftmost) odd entry. The entry at position $c-1$ is even and the entry at $c$ is odd. The entry at $c$ is the sum of two of the three numbers above it, at positions $c-1,c,c+1$ of row $n-1$. If those three had the same parity, every sum of two of them would be even, contradiction. So the three above contain a switch pair, occupying positions $j,j+1$ with $c\in\{j,j+1\}$.

Assign this switch pair of row $n-1$ to the run. Two different runs have first positions $c\ne c'$ that are not adjacent (there is an even entry between runs), so a single switch pair $\{j,j+1\}$ cannot be assigned to both (that would need $c=j$ and $c'=j+1$). Hence $R\le$ (number of switch pairs in row $n-1$), and the number of switch pairs in row $n$, $2R$, is at most twice the number in row $n-1$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2004-team-08.title: Apply the identity repeatedly
hmmt-feb-2004-team-08.body:
Let $x=a\star b$. By the given identity, $x\star x=b\star a$. Applying the identity to the pair $(b,a)$ gives $(b\star a)\star(b\star a)=a\star b$. Substituting $b\star a=x\star x$:
$$a\star b=(b\star a)\star(b\star a)=(x\star x)\star(x\star x).$$
The identity with $(a,b)=(x,x)$ says $(x\star x)\star(x\star x)=x\star x$. Therefore
$$a\star b=x\star x=(a\star b)\star(a\star b)=b\star a.\ ∎$$

hmmt-feb-2004-team-09.title: Direct
hmmt-feb-2004-team-09.body: If $b\in T$, then $b=a\star a$ for some $a\in S$. By the given identity with both elements equal to $a$, $(a\star a)\star(a\star a)=a\star a$, i.e. $b\star b=b$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2004-team-10.title: Use associativity and idempotence
hmmt-feb-2004-team-10.body:
Write $c=a\star b$ with $b\in T$. Since $a\in T$, $a\star a=a$. Then
$$a\star c=a\star(a\star b)=(a\star a)\star b=a\star b=c.\ ∎$$

hmmt-feb-2004-team-11.title: Minimal image
hmmt-feb-2004-team-11.body:
We know: $\star$ is commutative; every $b\in T$ satisfies $b\star b=b$.

*$T$ is closed under $\star$.* For $a,b\in T$: $(a\star b)\star(a\star b)=a\star a\star b\star b$ (by commutativity and associativity) $=a\star b$, so $a\star b=(a\star b)\star(a\star b)\in T$.

For $x\in T$ let $I(x)=\{x\star b:b\in T\}\subseteq T$ be its image. It contains $x=x\star x$. Facts: if $c\in I(x)$ then $x\star c=c$ (previous problem).

Since $T$ is finite, choose $a\in T$ with $|I(a)|$ as small as possible. Let $c\in I(a)$. We show $I(c)\subseteq I(a)$: if $d\in I(c)$, say $d=c\star e$ with $e\in T$, then $c\star d=c\star c\star e=d$, and $a\star c=c$, so $a\star d=a\star(c\star d)=(a\star c)\star d=c\star d=d$; as $d\in T$, $d=a\star d\in I(a)$.

Since $c\in T$ and $a$ was chosen with the smallest image, $|I(c)|\ge|I(a)|$, so $I(c)=I(a)$. In particular $a\in I(a)=I(c)$, so $a=c\star b'$ for some $b'\in T$. Then $c\star a=c\star(c\star b')=(c\star c)\star b'=c\star b'=a$. By commutativity and $a\star c=c$, we get $c=a\star c=c\star a=a$.

So $I(a)=\{a\}$, i.e. $a\star b=a$ for every $b\in T$ (note $a\star b\in T$ as $T$ is closed). ∎

hmmt-feb-2004-team-11.title: Alternative: multiply all elements of $T$
hmmt-feb-2004-team-11.body: $T$ is closed under $\star$ (shown above), and $\star$ is commutative and associative. List the elements of $T$ as $a_1,\dots,a_k$ (finite) and put $a=a_1\star a_2\star\cdots\star a_k\in T$; the value does not depend on the order. For $b\in T$, $a=c\star b$ where $c$ is the $\star$-product of all the other elements (if $k=1$ the claim is trivial). Then $a\star b=(c\star b)\star b=c\star(b\star b)=c\star b=a$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2004-team-12.title: The same element works
hmmt-feb-2004-team-12.body:
Let $a\in T$ with $a\star t=a$ for all $t\in T$, and let $b\in S$. By the given identity and commutativity/associativity,
$$a\star b=(b\star a)\star(b\star a)=b\star a\star b\star a=(a\star a)\star(b\star b).$$
Now $a\star a=a$ and $b\star b\in T$, so the right side equals $a\star(b\star b)=a$. Hence $a\star b=a$ for every $b\in S$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2004-team-13.title: Count even numbers by greatest odd divisor
hmmt-feb-2004-team-13.body:
For a real $x\ge1$, $\lfloor\log_2x\rfloor$ is the number of integers $e\ge1$ with $2^e\le x$. So for odd $k\le n$, $\lfloor\log_2(n/k)\rfloor=\#\{e\ge1:2^ek\le n\}$, which is the number of even integers $m\le n$ whose greatest odd divisor is $k$ (these are exactly $m=2^ek$ with $e\ge1$).

Every even $m\le n$ has a unique greatest odd divisor $k$, which is odd and at most $n$. Summing over all odd $k\le n$ therefore counts every even number $m\le n$ exactly once. As $n$ is odd, the number of even numbers in $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is $\frac{n-1}2$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2004-team-14.title: Swap the order of summation
hmmt-feb-2004-team-14.body:
$\sigma(i)$ is the sum of all $d\mid i$. Summing over $i\le n$, each $d\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ appears once for each multiple of $d$ that is at most $n$, i.e. $\lfloor n/d\rfloor$ times. So
$$\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma(i)=\sum_{d=1}^nd\left\lfloor\frac nd\right\rfloor\le\sum_{d=1}^nd\cdot\frac nd=\sum_{d=1}^nn=n^2.\ ∎$$

hmmt-feb-2004-team-15.title: Reciprocals of divisors
hmmt-feb-2004-team-15.body:
If $d\mid i$ then $i/d\mid i$ as well, and $\frac{i/d}{i}=\frac1d$. Hence $\frac{\sigma(i)}i=\sum_{d\mid i}\frac1d$.

Summing over $i\le n$ and swapping the order, $\frac1d$ occurs $\lfloor n/d\rfloor$ times (once per multiple of $d$ up to $n$):
$$\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\sigma(i)}i=\sum_{d=1}^n\frac1d\left\lfloor\frac nd\right\rfloor\le\sum_{d=1}^n\frac n{d^2}=n\left(1+\sum_{d=2}^n\frac1{d^2}\right).$$
Finally $\sum_{d=2}^n\frac1{d^2}<\sum_{d=2}^n\frac1{(d-1)d}=\sum_{d=2}^n\left(\frac1{d-1}-\frac1d\right)=1-\frac1n<1$, so the sum is less than $n\cdot2=2n$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2004-team-16.title: Rewrite as a sum over even numbers
hmmt-feb-2004-team-16.body:
As before, $\lfloor\log_2(n/k)\rfloor$ is the number of even $m\le n$ with greatest odd divisor $k$. For such $m=2^ek$, the odd divisors of $m$ are exactly the divisors of $k$, so $\sigma(k)$ is the sum of the odd divisors of $m$. Hence the left side equals
$$\sum_{\substack{m\le n\\ m\text{ even}}}\ \sum_{\substack{d\mid m\\ d\text{ odd}}}d=\sum_{d\text{ odd}}d\cdot\#\{\text{even }m\le n:d\mid m\}=\sum_{d\text{ odd}}d\left\lfloor\frac n{2d}\right\rfloor,$$
since the even multiples of the odd number $d$ are the multiples of $2d$.

*Bounding.* Because $n$ is odd, the largest multiple of $2d$ not exceeding $n$ is at most $n-1$, so $\lfloor\frac n{2d}\rfloor\le\frac{n-1}{2d}$ and each term is at most $\frac{n-1}2$. Only odd $d\le\frac n2$ contribute (otherwise the floor is $0$). Let $m$ be the largest odd integer less than $\frac n2$; the contributing $d$ are $1,3,\dots,m$, which are $\frac{m+1}2$ numbers. So the sum is at most $\frac{n-1}{2}\cdot\frac{m+1}{2}=\frac{(n-1)(m+1)}4$. Since $m\le\frac{n-1}2$, we have $m+1\le\frac{n+1}2$, and the sum is at most $\frac{(n-1)(n+1)}8=\frac{n^2-1}8<\frac{n^2}8$. ∎
